newsitem.title: UK: UK mortgage tax change hits poor hardest - lenders.
newsitem.headline: UK mortgage tax change hits poor hardest - lenders.

text.p: Britain's biggest mortgage lenders gave Chancellor Gordon Brown's first budget a cautious welcome on Wednesday, but said changes to mortgage interest tax relief (MIRAS) would hit poorest borrowers hardest.

"We are pleased the Chancellor has chosen to only reduce mortgage interest tax relief by five percent, this will minimise the impact on the housing market," said David Gilchrist, spokesman for Britain's largest mortgage lender Halifax Plc.

But Gilchrist called the effect of the move regressive. "This will hit poorer borrowers hardest," he said, adding someone with a 30,000 pound($49,700) mortgage would pay five percent more while someone with a 100,000 pound loan will pay 1.5 percent more.
And Abbey National Plc said it was disappointed by the Labour government's decision to cut MIRAS to 10 percent from 15 percent as of April 1998.
"We are disappointed that the typical homeowner will face an extra 10 pound charge from next April," and Abbey National spokesperson told Reuters.
But the bank, Britain's second largest home lender, said it was relieved MIRAS had not been totally abolished, as had been widely rumoured ahead of the budget.
Brown stressed he did not want Britain's housing market, which has shown recent signs of strength after the crash of the late 1980s and early 1990s, to return to the boom in prices which preceded it.
"I will not allow house prices to get out of control and put at risk the sustainability of the recovery," Brown told Parliament.
He was praised by home builder George Wimpey Plc which said the move would not dampen a much needed recovery in parts of Britain, particularly the north of England and Scotland.

"Our experience has taught us that economic confidence is the most important factor in the housing market," Wimpey's chairman Joe Dwyer said in a statement welcoming Brown's "pragmatic budget" and its focus on long-term stability.
Dwyer said Brown's decision not to remove MIRAS altogether was prudent as the benefit was significant not only for first time buyers but for those buying their homes on lower incomes.

Halifax's Gilchrist said the bank, which recently floated on the London stock exchange, would have liked to have seen an indication that the money saved by the measures would fund a mortgage benefit scheme.
"We continue to hope for this," he said.
John Caine of Alliance & Leicester said the budget showed the government recognised the importance of the housing market and making sure it did not get out of control.
He said the April 1998 date for the cut in MIRAS would give people time to adjust to the increased cost.

MIRAS is currently available on the first 30,000 pounds of a mortgage. Reducing it to 10 percent should generate some 900 million pounds for the Treasury, at a cost to each of Britain's 10 million homeowners of up to 10 pounds a month.
The Nationwide Building Society, now Britain's largest, said it would be helpful if the government clarified if it planned to phase out the tax relief over the next few years.

It too called for the introduction of a mortgage benefit scheme to help low income house owners, giving them assistance with mortgage costs in the same way as low income tenants get help in paying their rent.

Nationwide said that by only increasing stamp duty -- the tax paid when a property is bought -- on properties worth more than 250,000 pounds, the government had targeted those who could most afford the extra cost.
"Also these increases will primarily affect the housing market in London and the South East where the recovery has been strongest," it added.

None of the lenders said the increase in stamp duty, to 1.5 percent from one percent on property sales above 250,000 pounds and to two percent on purchases of more than 500,000 pounds, would have a significant effect on the housing market.
Halifax's Gilchrist said outside London price rises for houses were still modest and transaction levels were "below the norm for a healthy market".

Meanwhile Abbey National continues to predict 1997 will be the best year of the decade for the level of housing transactions, but says it will be substantially lower than during the boom period of the late 1980s.
Nationwide also raised the possibility of further interest rate rises which it said were heightened by no tax measures to limit consumer spending appearing in the budget. ($ = 0.602 British Pounds)
